guideTitle: Best Food Processors with Dicing Kits (2026)
metaTitle: Best Food Processors with Dicing Kits (2026)
metaDescription: Four food processors that include a real dicing kit, from Breville Paradice 9 and 16 to the KitchenAid 14-cup and a commercial Waring, compared and explained.
expertTake: The Breville Paradice 16 is the top pick because its dicing kit, 16-cup bowl and onboard storage are designed as one system. The KitchenAid KFP1466CU is the value pick for cooks who want dicing plus a proven adjustable slicer. Anyone who dices only a few times a year should skip the category and use a knife.
introParagraphs: Dicing is the cut that separates a premium processor from an ordinary one, and it is the job that most often sends cooks back to the cutting board. Slicing and shredding are common, but a grid that turns a slice into even cubes in one pass is a specialist tool, and few machines include one.

Because the kit is the whole point, we limited this guide to machines that really ship with a dicer, then compared how the kit works, how many sizes it cuts, how it is stored and how much food the bowl can hold.

products.name: Breville Paradice 16 BFP838 Processor and Dicer
products.description:
The Paradice 16 is the machine built around dicing. The kit ships in the box and includes multiple dice sizes, with the 16 mm and 12 mm cubes named in the listing, so you can cut chunky vegetables for stew and smaller cubes for salsa. A 16-cup bowl means a full batch of onions or potatoes fits without rounds.

Breville presents the machine as a system: precision, consistent size and presentation. That shows in the way the dicer and discs are stored together on the machine. Compared with the 9-cup Paradice, you get a bigger bowl and more capacity, which matters if you cook for a crowd.

It is a large, heavy machine, and the kit has more parts than most. Dice a flat-ended piece of produce, feed it with light pressure and brush the grid right after use, because wet starch hardens in the openings. Store the grid in its holder so the blades do not sit loose. Cut onions in half through the root and set them flat side down on the pusher, and trim a thin slice from round potatoes so they sit steady instead of rolling. The machine rewards a little preparation with remarkably even cubes that cook at the same rate, which is the real payoff of a dicer.
products.bestFor: Serious cooks who dice often and want the largest bowl with the kit included.
pros: Dicing kit ships in the box
Multiple dice sizes including 16 mm and 12 mm
cons: Large, heavy and needs counter space
Dicing grid needs prompt careful cleaning

products.name: Breville Paradice 9 BFP638 Processor and Dicer
products.description:
This is the compact version of the same idea. The bowl is nine cups, but the integrated caddy holds the dicing kit and discs on the machine, which makes it the easiest dicer to live with in a small kitchen. The listing describes it as precision and performance in a compact design, and that is a fair summary.

Beside the Paradice 16, you lose seven cups of bowl, so a big batch means two rounds. In exchange you gain a smaller footprint and a shorter lift. For a household of two or three it is plenty, and the dicing still works the same way.

It also comes in several colors, which are the same machine in a different finish. Dice trimmed produce, flat side down, and clean the grid with a brush straight away. Dry the parts completely before returning them to the caddy so nothing spots. Because the dicer has to be fed vertically through a small opening, long carrots and celery should be cut into pieces that match the chute height first. Many owners keep this smaller unit on the counter for daily use and find that it earns its space precisely because the kit is always at hand.
products.bestFor: Small kitchens that want dicing and tidy onboard storage in a 9-cup body.
pros: Integrated caddy holds the dicing kit
Same dicing system as the larger model
Brushed stainless is easy to wipe
cons: Nine cups needs rounds for big batches
Fewer cups than most full-size rivals

products.name: KitchenAid KFP1466CU 14-Cup with Exact Slice and Dicing Kit
products.description:
KitchenAid pairs its dicing kit with an adjustable Exact Slice system, and that combination is what makes this machine appealing. A lever on the outside of the bowl changes the slice thickness from thick to thin without opening the lid. Add a dicing kit and the same machine slices, shreds and cubes.

The 14-cup bowl is the second largest here, and a 2-in-1 wide-mouth feed tube takes large pieces. Speeds are simple: Low, High and Pulse. Against the Breville Paradice 16, the KitchenAid costs less and relies on a familiar KitchenAid design instead of a purpose-built dicing system.

There is also a renewed version of the same model sold separately, which is a good reminder to check the seller. Hand-wash the dicing grid and discs, top-rack the bowl and lid, and keep the lever free of crumbs so the slicing thickness moves smoothly. For dicing, set the slicer to the thickness that matches the grid, since a slice thicker than the grid height jams in the chute. Cooks who also bake will appreciate that the same machine kneads, so it can replace two appliances on a crowded counter.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want adjustable slicing and dicing in one machine at a lower tier than Breville.
pros: Exact Slice lever adjusts thickness externally
Simple Low, High and Pulse controls
cons: Dicing is an add-on to a general design

products.name: Waring WFP16SCD 4-Quart Continuous-Feed with Dicing
products.description:
This is a commercial machine, and it belongs in a different category from the home units. A two-horsepower motor drives a four-quart batch bowl, which is roughly sixteen cups, and the continuous-feed head lets the machine dice, slice and shred a steady stream of produce directly into a container.

The LiquiLock system seals the batch bowl so soups, sauces and dressings can be processed without leaks. The listing counts over twenty processing options including dicing, shredding, slicing, chopping, pureeing and emulsifying. That versatility is great for a restaurant or a serious home cook who preps in volume.

It is heavy, loud and built for daily service rather than a home counter. Expect a large footprint and a more involved cleanup. Disassemble the continuous-feed head after each session, wash every part and dry it fully, and check that the bowl seal is seated before you run a liquid batch. Plan a dedicated spot with enough clearance for the continuous-feed head, since the tall assembly will not slide under a standard cabinet. Home cooks who buy it are usually running a small catering side business or preserving large harvests, where a motor that never strains is worth the footprint.
products.bestFor: Cooks who prep in volume and want commercial power with continuous-feed dicing.
pros: 2 HP motor is the strongest here
cons: Heavy, loud and bulky for a home kitchen
Cleanup takes longer than a home unit

buyingCriteria.explanation: A dicing kit is a grid plus a slicing disc that cuts a slice into cubes. The Breville Paradice 16 lists the 16 mm and 12 mm sizes, while the KitchenAid KFP1466CU includes a dicing kit with its Exact Slice system. Always confirm the kit is in the box, because some listings sell the dicer as a separate accessory. A bare Breville dicing kit is sold on its own for people who already own a compatible machine, which is a useful reminder that a processor and a dicer are not always bundled together.

Different recipes want different cubes: large for stew, medium for chili, small for salsa. Machines with more than one dice size, such as the Paradice 16, are more flexible. A single size works only if it matches your recipes. If your favorite dishes call for a fine dice, a coarse-only kit will leave you chopping by hand again, so check the sizes before you commit to a model.

Batch machines like the Breville and KitchenAid dice what fits in the chute and then stop. The Waring's continuous-feed head dices a steady stream into a container. Choose continuous feed only if you routinely dice pounds of produce. A home cook who dices two onions and a pepper for dinner gains nothing from a commercial head and gives up cabinet space and a quick cleanup.

A 16-cup bowl on the Paradice 16 swallows a whole batch, while the 9-cup Paradice 9 needs two rounds. The 14-cup KitchenAid sits in between. Match the bowl to your largest regular batch, not your average one. A dicer-driven recipe such as a big pot of chili or a tray of roasted vegetables usually uses three or four onions and peppers, which is why the 9-cup models can feel tight.
A dicing grid has fine blades that must be stored safely. The Paradice 9 and 16 include onboard storage for the kit, which reduces lost parts. Loose grids in drawers are a hazard and easy to damage.

Wet starch dries hard in grid openings, so a brush straight after use is essential. Flat-ended produce feeds more cleanly and leaves less residue. A dishwasher is hard on fine grid edges. Poke the grid out with the supplied cleaning tool or the blunt end of a wooden skewer, working from the cutting side toward the back, so the fragments push out the way they came in.

howWeEvaluated.title: Kit verification
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked that each machine ships with a dicing kit or lists it as included. Listings that sell the dicer separately were excluded, which is why a standalone kit accessory is not among the picks. We also noted which dice sizes are named, along with whether the kit stores on the machine, and we treated a kit that lists several sizes as more flexible than one that lists none.

howWeEvaluated.title: Dicing quality design
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared grid design, feed method and slice control. The Breville's purpose-built kit and the KitchenAid's Exact Slice earned credit, and the Waring's continuous feed earned credit for volume.

howWeEvaluated.title: Capacity and rounds
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched bowl volume, from 9 cups to roughly 16 cups, to typical dicing batches. Larger bowls ranked higher for volume.

howWeEvaluated.title: Storage and cleaning
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at onboard storage and how hard the grid is to clean. A caddy that holds every part ranked higher than loose accessories, because the grid is the most fragile and most expensive piece to replace. We also looked at how many separate steps it takes to take the kit apart and wash it.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value across the tier
howWeEvaluated.description: We ordered the four by price tier. The KitchenAid sits lowest, the Breville models in the middle and the Waring at the top.

cards.label: Batch bowl
cards.text: The Breville and KitchenAid models dice what fits in the chute and stop. They suit home cooks.

cards.label: Continuous feed
cards.text: The Waring dices a steady stream into a container. It suits high-volume prep.

howToChoose.note: Pick a batch bowl for home cooking, and continuous feed only for large daily volumes. A batch bowl is also easier to clean and far quieter, which matters more in a house than in a commercial kitchen.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A small dice size, flat-ended produce and a bowl you can empty quickly. Salsa needs smaller cubes and gentle pressure, and tomatoes are best de-seeded and pressed lightly so they cut rather than crush. For mirepoix, dice onion, carrot and celery separately because each has a different firmness, then combine them in the pan.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Breville Paradice models with multiple dice sizes are the best fit, and the KitchenAid is the budget alternative.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You dice every week or cook for crowds. The Paradice 16 or Waring repay the cost.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You dice occasionally. The KitchenAid KFP1466CU gives dicing at the lowest tier.

maintenance.why: Starch dries hard in the grid openings. A soft brush clears it quickly.

Dishwashers can dull and bend fine edges, and a bent grid produces ragged cubes that no amount of pressure will fix. Hand washing with warm soapy water and a soft brush keeps the cuts crisp for years.
Onboard storage prevents lost parts and keeps the fine blades from knocking against other metal. Dry parts fully first so moisture does not sit in the caddy and spot the stainless.

A seal that is not seated leaks, and a leak into the motor housing is the fastest way to ruin a commercial machine. Wipe the groove, re-seat the seal and run a short water test before the first soup of the day.

Crumbs and dried juice can stiffen the slicing lever over time. Wipe around it with a damp cloth and check that it moves through its full range without sticking, because a stiff lever is a sign of residue rather than wear.

faq.a: A dicing kit is a grid and slicing disc that cut a slice into cubes in one pass. It needs trimmed produce and gentle pressure. It replaces a lot of knife work, and the cubes come out the same size, so a pan of onions or peppers cooks evenly instead of leaving some pieces raw and others browned.

faq.q: Does the KitchenAid KFP1466CU include the dicer?
faq.a: The listing describes the model as having the Exact Slice system and a dicing kit. Confirm that the kit is in the box when you buy. A renewed listing of the same model is also sold.

faq.q: Is a Breville Paradice worth the cost?
faq.a: If you dice weekly it saves a lot of time. If you only dice occasionally, the premium is hard to justify. A knife is fine for rare dicing. A useful test is to count how many times in the last month you cut vegetables into cubes: if it was more than a handful, a dicing machine will pay for itself in time saved, and if not, the money is better spent on a good chef knife.

faq.q: Can I dice soft vegetables like tomatoes?
faq.a: Soft vegetables crush in a dicing grid. Slice them instead, or chill them first. Firm onions, peppers and potatoes dice best. Carrots and celery work well when cut to fit the chute, while cucumbers and zucchini release water and are better sliced thick, patted dry and cut by hand if you need cubes.

faq.q: Is the Waring too much for home use?
faq.a: For most home cooks, yes. It is built for commercial volume and is heavy and loud. It suits serious cooks who prep large amounts. If you are tempted by the power, picture the cleanup after a single batch of onions and ask whether you would do that weekly; if the answer is no, a Breville or KitchenAid is the better fit.

faq.q: How do I clean the dicing grid?
faq.a: Brush it under running water right after use and hand-wash it, pushing debris out in the direction opposite to the cutting path. Use a soft brush so the openings clear without damage. Dry it before storing.
